Unmarked users,

I am using the modSel() function to extract AIC values from 48 permutations of a model fit with pcountOpen. If I inspect the results from each model, remove the one that did not converge, and then run the modSel() function again it works fine and the AIC values (among other statistics) are printed in a table.  Is there a way to trap this error in the modSel() function so the user doesn't have to manually inspect each model?

I'm running R 2.14.1 with Unmarked v. 0.9-4

Thanks,
Jason

Yes they do, but I don't inspect the model summaries before extracting the

independent variables with the three distributions), run the models and
assign the output to an object (without having the model summary print to

values I will then inspect summaries of the "best" models (change in AIC <
2).

time of year, at the same sites, with the same gear, and protocol for
multiple consecutive years.  I am trying to determine what factors (e.g.
area, conductivity, turbidity, and crew leader) affect detectability of the
different fish species we encounter using the pcountOpen model.  I believe
that the schooling species violate an assumption of the Dail-Madsen model
and the abundance estimates appear unreasonable.  However, abundance and
detection estimates for two of the non-schooling species are in line with
the estimates from depletion surveys I conducted the past 2 years in the
same stream, but different sites, and same electrofishing gear.

Jason

When I estimate density, I get a number that I can pass on to land managers and tell them that there are ~130 individuals per hectare at site X. I like the straight forward interpretation of that number. But I don't understand what exactly the abundance estimate means. Any insight would be greatly appreciated.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Definition of abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

The estimate you get from distsamp when output="abund" is simply the expected number of individuals/plot. If you recorded data out to 100 meters, then the estimate would be the expected number of individuals in a 100 meter radius plot. Density is just N/plot area.

Richard

messages.subject: distsamp vs. DISTANCE with hierarchical sampling design
messages.subject_clean: distsamp vs. DISTANCE with hierarchical sampling design
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm a relatively new to unmarked, so please forgive my likely
clumsiness. I'm attempting to use distsamp to repeat some previously
conducted analyses from DISTANCE and running into some trouble.

The data are structured as follows: point counts were conducted at 36
sites with multiple points within each site. Points were visited
multiple times over the course of a summer.

I am able to get unmarked and DISTANCE to agree (exactly) under the
following conditions:
1. I use a site- and visit-specific (site and visit seem to define a
"stratum" in Distance) detection function and density estimate in
DISTANCE.
2. I narrow the dataset in R to include only a single visit to a
single site and use a null model in distsamp.
3. As a result the density and the parameters of the detection
function for the visit and site modeled in unmarked will match those
from DISTANCE.

I have been unable to make any headway at replicating the results at
higher levels of the sample hierarchy, despite trying to use distsamp
on all visits to a single site with Visit as a covariate and to the
entire data set. I recognize this issue has come up before, but it
didn't seem to come to any concrete resolution in terms of how to go
about specifying the model to make them reproducible across programs.

Thanks for any guidance!
Joshua Goldberg

messages.subject: Differences between "unmarked" and R code in Kéry et al. 2005
messages.subject_clean: Differences between "unmarked" and R code in Kéry et al. 2005
messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody, I am a new unmarked-member and I would like to have your
advice.
A couple of years ago I analysed a dataset of repeated point counts of
different deer species, and I used the R code provided by Kéry et al.
(2005 Ecological Applications) with satisfactory results.
Now I am trying to analyse the same dataset with the unmarked package,
and I found an important difference in the results:  when no
covariates are used, or covariates are used only to model abundance,
detection and lambda estimates are identical with the two methods, but
when covariates are added to model detectability the results of the
two methods diverge.

Has anybody used both methods and compared the results? I am pretty
sure this is my mistake, but I would like to be sure to use the right
code now (variables in the example are standardized, with zero-mean):

p3 <- pcount(~ hour  ~ perc_open, datiUMF, K = 100)
lc1 <- linearComb(p3, c(1, 0), type="det")
backTransform(lc1)
lc2 <- linearComb(p3, c(1, 0), type="state")
backTransform(lc2)

Thank you in advance,

Simona Imperio, PhD
ISAC-CNR
Italian National Research Council
C.so Fiume 4, I-10133 Torino, Italy

messages.subject: Re: RE : [unmarked] AICcmodavg
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

The "newdata" data.frame should contain the values of the covariates for which you want predictions. In your example, "a" has no values. They are all NA. I'm not familiar with your data, but if "Unit" is a factor with 3 levels, say "a", "b", and "c", then you could do something like this:

newdata <- data.frame(Unit=c("a", "b", "c"))
predict(j4.h.list, type='state', newdata = newdata)

or, if you want a prediction for a single level, try this:

newdata <- data.frame(Unit=factor("a", levels=c("a", "b", "c")))
predict(j4.h.list, type='state', newdata = newdata)

Hope this helps.

Richard

messages.subject: pcount vs occuRN
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

I have a simple question: how to assess which type of model (Royle Biometrics or Royle-Nichols) is the better choice for my dataset?

I am trying to estimate bear abundance using track counts on 2-km stretches of forest roads in the Carpathians. There are 36 transects with 4 visits per transect. There are a lot of zeroes, and the track counts are low, ranging between 1 and 3 (mostly 1s). The occuRN models use the count data truncated to 1s.

So far I used model averaging for sets of pcount and occuRN models separately, and I obtain slightly different estimates of abundance. Can I select which models perform better by just comparing AIC values of occuRN and pcount models? I am basically using the same dataset for both types of models, but I was not sure if using AIC to compare across different types of models is correct.

Thank you...

Best,
Viorel

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] pcount vs occuRN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Viorel,
 you should use the pcount() function which fits the N-mixture model.  It probably isn't possible to compare the AIC because the likelihoods are scaled differently between the two models. In any case, the RN model assumes a binary observation whereas the N-mixture model the observation has support 0,1,2,3,...., which matches up with your situation.
regards
andy

messages.subject: Distance Sampling Stratification
messages.body_plain:
Greetings. I have an analysis which I have recently completed in
Program Distance. I am converting it over to the package unmarked in
the hopes of using the results in a broader hierarchical analysis. So
far, I have been successful in producing consistent results for the
entire study area estimates.

In program distance I am using all samples to produce the detection
function, however I have 24 separate territories where I would like to
produce stratified density estimates. So far, in unmarked I haven't
seen an obvious way to do this. When I use predict, I do get 24
answers, but they are all identical.

Is there a particular way to set this up? One thought I had was to
include the territory ID as a covariate, then use backTranformation
and LinearComb to explore the results, but this doesn't seem right.

Any pointers would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.
